title: Standard Curve (Calibration Curve)

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM, CLSI)

summary: A curve generated by measuring a series of samples with known, precisely prepared concentrations, used to convert a raw instrument signal from an unknown sample into a calculated concentration.
explanation: Most quantitative assays (spectrophotometric protein/nucleic acid assays, ELISA, qPCR) do not measure concentration directly — they measure a proxy signal (absorbance, fluorescence, a cycle threshold) that is related to concentration but is not the same thing. A standard curve is built by plotting that signal against a set of known standard concentrations spanning the expected range of the unknowns, then fitting a mathematical relationship (often linear, but not always) to that data. Unknown samples are then read against this curve — but only reliably within the range actually covered by the standards; extrapolating far beyond the tested standard range assumes the same relationship holds outside the region that was actually verified, which is often not a safe assumption.

comparison.aspect: Interpolation (unknown falls within the standard range)
comparison.example: A generally well-supported estimate, assuming the standards themselves were prepared and measured correctly

comparison.aspect: Extrapolation (unknown falls outside the standard range)
comparison.example: Unreliable — the true relationship outside the tested range is unverified and the sample should instead be diluted/concentrated to fall within range and re-measured

commonMisconceptions: Reading an unknown's concentration off a standard curve when its signal falls outside the range actually tested by the standards.
Assuming a standard curve fit is universally linear without checking — some assays are only linear over a limited range and curve at the extremes.
